name: Prayer camps, faith and traditional healers for mental illness
what_people_do: Families take people with psychosis or severe distress to a traditional healer, prayer camp or church; some centres use shackling, flogging and forced fasting.
why_they_say_it_works: Illness is seen as spiritual, so prayer, ritual and herbs are the first treatment; healers are trusted and close by.

documented_by.source: Lambert JE et al 2020, Glob Ment Health, PMID 33123375
documented_by.quote_or_summary: Ghana: 82 people treated in healing centres and 40 healers interviewed; most believed mental illness has a spiritual cause; about 30.5% of those treated were exposed to maltreatment, yet half would return; healers using shackling believed it necessary; most healers were willing to collaborate with the health system.

documented_by.source: Ayinde OO et al 2023, Transcult Psychiatry, PMID 34913379
documented_by.quote_or_summary: Ibadan, Kumasi and Nairobi, 85 people who had used traditional and faith healers for psychosis: supernatural causes predominant; prayer and rituals central; concurrent or consecutive use of conventional care was common.

evidence.tested: Outcomes of care in healing centres
evidence.finding: Maltreatment in about 30%, trauma history linked to worse symptoms; no outcome trial.

source.name: Lambert JE et al 2020, Glob Ment Health, PMID 33123375

harm_note: Shackling, flogging and forced fasting are documented in these centres. Collaboration with clinics is possible and wanted by many healers.
gaps: No trial of faith healing outcomes found.
Prevalence of use by country not extracted.
